rationale: All three lenses ran as independent subagents with parseable output against a spec, and the batched reachability verifier simulated each candidate against the real code; no lens failed and the diff needed no sharding. Two blocking findings survive, both newly introduced by the Task 5 dedup precedence flip and both rooted in the same unconditional collision replacement: a shadowing org entry is reverted to the bundled public URL on a transient fetch failure (violating acceptance criterion 6, which the acceptance lens passed only because the existing regression test does not construct the shadowing case), and a colliding backend entry with no OAuth config silently downgrades a bundled default's oauth:true. 5 findings were deferred as real but pre-existing and out of this change's scope (partial-validation revocation; unnormalized URL collision allowing double registration; authorizationUrl/tokenUrl accepted as any non-empty string with no scheme check; callbackHost not loopback-restricted; org catalog not deduped against itself) and are recorded in docs/superpowers/tasks/2026-08-11-epmcdme-14072-extend-the-codemie-cli-s-managed-mcp/code-review-deferred.md; 13 candidates were dismissed as unreachable or below the blocking floor.

findings.title: A transient fetch failure reverts a shadowing org entry to the bundled public URL
findings.problem: The dedup flip lets a backend entry suppress a bundled default by name or URL, but nothing records that the suppression happened. When a later fetch fails, `org` becomes `[]` (desktop.ts:552), so `defaultsDeduped` restores every bundled default, and because `orgFetchSucceeded` is false `previouslyManagedNames` is `[]` (desktop.ts:562). `reconcileManagedMcpServers` then treats the bundled name as owned and drops the user's existing internal entry in its favour. Verifier simulation: run 1 writes org `{name:'notion', url:'https://mcp.internal.corp/notion'}`; run 2 with a failed fetch leaves the config holding the bundled `Notion` at `https://mcp.notion.com/mcp`.
findings.impact: Violates acceptance criterion 6 — a transient backend outage must never revoke a previously-managed org entry. Worse than a plain revocation: the tenant's internal MCP server is silently replaced by a public third-party endpoint of the same name, so the client keeps working while pointing somewhere the tenant did not intend. Newly introduced by this change — before the flip the colliding org entry was dropped at run 1 and could never be written, so the scenario did not exist.
findings.recommendation: Make the failed-fetch path preserve a previously-shadowed default rather than restoring it. Options: persist the set of suppressed default names alongside `managedNames` in the marker state and continue to filter those defaults while `orgFetchSucceeded` is false; or skip the bundled-default restoration entirely on a failed fetch, consistent with the existing rule that a failed fetch changes nothing. Cover it with a two-run test — successful shadowing fetch, then a null fetch — asserting the internal URL survives.

findings.title: Collision replacement has no auth-shape guard, so a backend entry can downgrade a bundled default's oauth:true
findings.problem: `defaultsDeduped` (desktop.ts:557-559) drops a bundled default purely on a name or URL collision, with no comparison of the two entries' resolved auth. `isValidCanonicalEntry` makes both `oauth` and `auth` optional (managed-mcp-remote.ts:65-90), so a backend row such as `{name:'Notion', transport:'http', url:...}` validates cleanly and `resolveDesktopOAuth` falls through to `return false` (desktop.ts:278). The bundled entry's `oauth: true` is replaced by `oauth: false`.
findings.impact: Silently disables OAuth for that server — the exact defect class this ticket exists to fix, reintroduced through a different door. `summarizeManagedOauthShapes` does not catch it: it is computed over the org catalog only (index.ts:459), so the log looks identical whether or not a default's auth was suppressed. Newly introduced by the dedup flip.
findings.recommendation: Guard the replacement on auth: when a backend entry collides with a bundled default whose oauth is `true` or an object, and the backend entry resolves to `false`, keep the default (or at minimum log the downgrade loudly). Separately, compute the oauth-shape summary over the final written `managedSet` rather than the org catalog so any suppression is visible in the field.
